Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Hundreds of refugees on Wednesday blocked a main road in northwest Pakistan, to protest living conditions for some of the 1.5 million Pakistanis forced to flee their homes in the past three weeks. The refugee situation in Pakistan could be a bigger threat than fighting with Taliban, U.N. says. "The government has been making big promises, but none of those were ever fulfilled," said Hazrat Bilal, a protester and refugee whose family has taken up temporary residence in a primary school. The refugees had blocked the main road in Pakistan's Mardan district since 8 a.m. Wednesday, Bilal said by telephone. The demonstrators were demanding food, water and other government services, he said. Mardan is a main transit point for the large numbers of Pakistanis fleeing the Swat Valley, the site of fierce fighting between Taliban militants and Pakistani soldiers.  The first pictures from the fighting » . The refugee crisis could pose a bigger threat to stability in Pakistan than the war itself, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Antonio Guterres told CNN while touring a refugee camp in the nearby Swabi district last week. The Pakistani government has been working with international aid agencies to establish camps for refugees, where tents, food, water and basic medical services are provided. But the scale and speed of the displacement -- said to be the worst since the Rwandan genocide in 1994 -- have overwhelmed aid workers, Guterres said. "The scale of the problem is such that all our resources combined cannot cope with it. And it's very important for this population not to feel abandoned," Guterres said. "Without massive support of the international community for the Pakistani people, this will become a very dramatic problem, and not only a humanitarian problem." On Tuesday, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton announced $110 million in humanitarian aid for Pakistani refugees. She also unveiled a system that lets Americans donate to the U.N. refugee effort, by sending a text message on mobile phone, including the word "Swat." Meanwhile, Pakistan's military said it was continuing the assault on Taliban militants. Pakistani forces have targeted regional Taliban commander Maulana Fazlullah and Taliban spokesman Muslim Khan, but have "no information about whether we have been successful," said the spokesman, Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas. He said 80 "terrorists" were killed Tuesday night in "intense fighting" in the town of Sultanwas, located in Buner district. One Pakistani soldier was also killed in recent fighting, Abbas said.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — On Wednesday, several hundred displaced people shut down a major road in northwestern Pakistan, demonstrating against the conditions faced by some of the 1.5 million Pakistanis who have been driven from their homes over the previous three weeks.

The United Nations has warned that Pakistan’s refugee emergency may present an even greater danger than the conflict with the Taliban.

“The government has made many grand pledges, but not one of them has been carried out,” said Hazrat Bilal, a displaced protester whose family is temporarily living in a primary school.

Speaking by phone, Bilal said the refugees had been blocking the main road in Pakistan’s Mardan district since 8 a.m. Wednesday. He said the protesters were calling for food, water and other services from the government.

Mardan serves as a key transit hub for the many Pakistanis escaping the Swat Valley, where Pakistani troops and Taliban fighters have been engaged in heavy clashes.

During a visit last week to a refugee camp in the nearby district of Swabi, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Antonio Guterres told CNN that the displacement crisis could endanger Pakistan’s stability more than the fighting itself.

Pakistan’s government has been cooperating with international relief organizations to set up camps for displaced people, providing tents, food, water and basic health care. However, Guterres said aid workers have been unable to keep up with the size and rapid pace of the population movement, described as the largest displacement since the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

“The scale of the problem is such that all our resources combined cannot cope with it. And it’s very important for this population not to feel abandoned,” Guterres said. “Without massive support of the international community for the Pakistani people, this will become a very dramatic problem, and not only a humanitarian problem.”

On Tuesday, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said the United States would provide $110 million in humanitarian assistance for Pakistani refugees. She also introduced a method allowing Americans to contribute to the U.N. refugee response by sending a mobile-phone text message containing the word “Swat.”

At the same time, Pakistan’s military said its offensive against Taliban militants was still under way. Military spokesman Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas said Pakistani forces had gone after regional Taliban leader Maulana Fazlullah and Taliban spokesman Muslim Khan, but had “no information about whether we have been successful.”

Abbas also said that 80 “terrorists” were killed Tuesday night during “intense fighting” in Sultanwas, a town in Buner district. He added that one Pakistani soldier had also died in recent clashes.

The demonstration reflected growing frustration among displaced families who say they are struggling to survive after fleeing violence in the region.

In recent weeks, about 1.5 million Pakistanis have left their homes because of fighting between Taliban militants and Pakistani soldiers in the Swat Valley. Many of the displaced have sought shelter with relatives, in schools, or in crowded camps set up by aid groups and the government.

The United Nations has warned that Pakistan’s refugee crisis could become an even greater threat to the country’s stability than the fighting itself. Officials say the sudden movement of so many people has created an enormous humanitarian emergency, putting pressure on local communities, relief organizations, and government agencies.

Although aid agencies and Pakistani authorities have established camps and begun distributing supplies, the scale and speed of the displacement have overwhelmed available resources. Many refugees still lack reliable access to clean water, food, medical care, and sanitation.

In response to the crisis, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton announced $110 million in humanitarian aid for Pakistani refugees. The assistance is intended to help provide emergency relief, including food, shelter, water, and medical support, as Pakistan struggles to manage one of the largest displacement crises in its recent history.

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — Hundreds of Pakistanis displaced by fighting in the Swat Valley blocked a main road in the northwestern city of Mardan on Tuesday, protesting what they described as unbearable conditions in makeshift camps and a lack of food, water and shelter.

The demonstrators, many of whom fled a Pakistani military offensive against Taliban militants in Swat and surrounding districts, said they had been waiting for assistance for days in intense heat. Some chanted slogans against the government and demanded faster distribution of aid.

“We left everything behind to save our lives,” one displaced resident said. “Now our children are hungry, and there is no proper place to sleep.”

Mardan, in North West Frontier Province, has become one of the main destinations for families escaping the fighting. Schools, public buildings and tent camps have been packed with people who fled as troops moved into Taliban-held areas.

The United Nations has warned that the scale of the displacement is straining relief efforts. U.N. agencies have said hundreds of thousands of people need urgent shelter, clean water, sanitation and medical care, and that crowded camps could face disease outbreaks if supplies do not arrive quickly.

International aid officials have described the crisis as one of Pakistan’s largest internal displacements in recent years, with many families staying outside official camps with relatives or host communities, making them harder to reach.

In Washington, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton announced additional humanitarian assistance for Pakistanis uprooted by the conflict. Clinton said the United States would provide emergency aid including food, water, tents and medical supplies, and urged the international community to respond quickly.

The Pakistani military, meanwhile, said its operation in Swat and nearby areas was continuing. Army officials reported clashes with militants and said troops had killed a number of fighters while advancing into contested towns. The military has said it is trying to avoid civilian casualties, but the offensive has prompted a mass exodus from the valley.

Pakistan’s government says the campaign is necessary to push back Taliban militants who had expanded their control in Swat despite an earlier peace deal. But for the displaced, the immediate concern is survival.

“We want peace in Swat,” another protester in Mardan said. “But until then, we need help.”

**Refugees Protest as Pakistan Displacement Crisis Deepens Amid Taliban Offensive**

*Northwest Pakistan, 2009* — Thousands of Pakistanis displaced by fighting between government forces and Taliban militants protested in the country’s northwest, as aid agencies warned that the rapidly growing humanitarian crisis could threaten Pakistan’s stability.

The unrest comes as Pakistan’s army presses ahead with major operations against Taliban fighters in the Swat Valley and surrounding districts, including Buner and Lower Dir. The offensive has forced huge numbers of civilians to flee their homes, creating one of the country’s largest internal displacement crises in recent history.

At camps and registration centers across North West Frontier Province — now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — displaced families complained of severe shortages of food, water, shelter and medical care. Many said they had spent days traveling in extreme heat, often with little money and no certainty about when they could return home.

Some refugees staged protests over delays in aid distribution and overcrowded conditions, demanding better support from the government and international organizations.

“We left everything behind,” one displaced resident said. “Our homes, our crops, our animals — now we are waiting in lines for food and tents.”

The United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, warned that the scale of displacement was placing enormous pressure on host communities and could have consequences far beyond the immediate conflict zone. Officials said the crisis required urgent international assistance, noting that many families were not in formal camps but staying with relatives, in schools or in improvised shelters.

Aid agencies said the number of displaced people had risen sharply as fighting intensified, with estimates reaching well over one million and eventually approaching two million. Relief workers warned that shortages of sanitation, clean water and healthcare could lead to disease outbreaks, particularly among children and the elderly.

The Pakistani government has defended the military campaign as necessary to halt the Taliban’s advance and reassert state control in the northwest. The offensive followed a breakdown of a controversial peace deal in Swat, where militants had expanded their influence and imposed harsh rule in several areas.

Army officials said troops were targeting Taliban positions and attempting to minimize civilian casualties, but the fighting has left many towns deserted. Residents fleeing the area reported artillery fire, aerial bombardment and street battles.

The crisis has also raised political concerns. Analysts warned that if displaced families feel abandoned, anger toward the state could grow — potentially benefiting militant groups that have long exploited grievances in the region.

International donors have pledged support, but UN officials said funding remained insufficient for the scale of need. Humanitarian workers called for faster delivery of tents, food, medicine and cash assistance, as well as protection for civilians trapped in conflict areas.

For many families crowded into camps or sheltering with relatives, the immediate concern is survival. But the longer the displacement continues, the greater the challenge facing Pakistan: defeating the Taliban militarily while preventing a humanitarian emergency from becoming a broader national crisis.

**Hundreds of displaced Pakistanis block main road, demanding food, water and basic services**

Hundreds of displaced Pakistanis blocked a major road on Monday, demanding urgent access to food, clean water and basic services after being forced from their homes by worsening humanitarian conditions.

The protesters, including women and children, gathered along the roadway and halted traffic for several hours, saying they had received little or no assistance since arriving at temporary shelters. Many said they were struggling to find drinking water, medical care and sanitation facilities.

“We left everything behind, and now our children are hungry,” said one displaced man, who asked to be identified only as Ahmed for security reasons. “We are not asking for luxury. We need food, clean water and a safe place to live.”

Local authorities said they were aware of the protest and were working with aid organizations to assess needs and deliver supplies. Officials urged demonstrators to reopen the road, saying the blockade was disrupting emergency movement and local transport.

Pakistan has faced repeated displacement crises in recent years, driven by flooding, insecurity, economic hardship and climate-related disasters. Aid groups have warned that vulnerable communities often face overcrowded shelters, limited access to health care and rising food insecurity.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres has repeatedly called for stronger international support for Pakistan, particularly in the wake of climate-related disasters that have devastated communities across the country. Speaking previously about Pakistan’s humanitarian needs, Guterres said the country required “massive support” from the international community as it confronts the effects of displacement and climate shocks.

At the protest site, displaced families said they would continue their demonstration until officials provided concrete assistance.

“We have waited for days,” Ahmed said. “If no one listens, what choice do we have but to come to the road?”

Humanitarian agencies say immediate priorities include clean water, emergency food supplies, sanitation, medical services and shelter for families who have lost homes or livelihoods. Local officials said additional relief deliveries were expected, though it was not immediately clear when they would reach the affected families.

**ISLAMABAD —** Fighting between Pakistani forces and Taliban militants in the Swat Valley has triggered a deepening refugee crisis, with hundreds of thousands of civilians fleeing mountain towns and villages as the army presses a major offensive against insurgent strongholds.

Families packed into trucks, buses and private cars have streamed out of Swat and neighboring districts in recent days, many heading toward the northwestern towns of **Mardan** and **Swabi**, where authorities and aid groups are struggling to shelter displaced people in camps, schools and private homes.

Pakistani officials say the military operation is aimed at driving Taliban fighters from Swat, once a popular tourist destination, after militants expanded their control and challenged the government’s authority. The fighting has raised fears of a prolonged humanitarian emergency in a region already strained by poverty and insecurity.

The Pakistani military reported fresh casualties in the operation, saying troops had killed scores of militants while also suffering losses among soldiers. Independent confirmation of battlefield casualty figures was not immediately possible because access to the conflict zone remains restricted.

The United States has pledged emergency assistance to help Pakistan cope with the displaced population, including food, shelter materials and medical support. Washington has also backed Islamabad’s campaign against the Taliban, viewing the insurgency in northwestern Pakistan as a threat to regional stability and to efforts across the border in Afghanistan.

Aid workers warn that the scale of displacement is growing rapidly and that camps around Mardan and Swabi are under pressure as more families arrive with few possessions. Many refugees say they fled amid artillery fire, airstrikes and street battles, leaving behind homes, livestock and livelihoods.

Pakistani leaders have called on the public and international donors to support relief efforts, while insisting the offensive is necessary to restore government control. But the exodus from Swat has underscored the heavy civilian cost of the conflict and the challenges facing Pakistan as it confronts Taliban militants entrenched in parts of the northwest.

**Pakistan’s internal refugee emergency deepens as fighting spreads and aid agencies warn of breaking point**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistan’s rapidly escalating military campaign against Taliban militants in the northwest has triggered one of the country’s largest internal displacement crises in modern history, with overwhelmed relief agencies warning that hundreds of thousands of civilians are fleeing faster than authorities can shelter, feed or register them.

The exodus — driven by intense fighting in Swat Valley, Buner and neighboring districts of the North West Frontier Province, now known as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — has sent families pouring into schools, government buildings, relatives’ homes and crowded relief camps. Many fled with little more than the clothes they were wearing, leaving behind farms, shops, livestock and homes as Pakistani troops pressed an offensive aimed at pushing militants out of areas they had seized or threatened.

The United Nations and humanitarian groups say the scale and speed of the displacement have strained the emergency response to the limit. Aid workers have warned that camps are filling quickly, sanitation is deteriorating, and supplies of food, clean water, tents and medical care are struggling to keep pace.

At the same time, frustration among displaced families has begun spilling into public anger. In and around relief camps, some families have protested what they describe as poor conditions, slow registration, shortages of drinking water and inadequate food distribution. Many displaced people have complained of long waits in extreme heat, overcrowded tents and insufficient medical attention for children and the elderly.

“We left because there was shelling and fighting everywhere,” one displaced resident told local reporters near a camp in the northwest. “Now we are safe from bullets, but we have no water, no proper shelter and no idea when we can go home.”

### UN warns aid system is overwhelmed

United Nations officials have described the crisis as a major test for Pakistan’s civilian authorities and the international aid system. The number of internally displaced people surged dramatically in a matter of days as military operations intensified in Swat, Lower Dir and Buner districts.

Aid agencies warned that the influx was overwhelming existing capacity. Many of the displaced have avoided formal camps and instead moved in with relatives or host families, making them harder to identify and assist. That has complicated efforts to distribute food and supplies and raised fears that the true scale of the emergency is even larger than official camp figures suggest.

UN agencies and partner organizations have appealed for urgent international funding, saying they need resources not only for emergency shelter and food but also for sanitation, vaccinations, maternal care and trauma support. Humanitarian officials have also warned that poor conditions in crowded camps could lead to outbreaks of disease, especially among children.

The crisis has placed additional pressure on Pakistan’s government, which is trying to show that it can both fight militants and protect civilians displaced by the offensive. Pakistani officials have said they are working to expand camps and provide assistance, but acknowledge the unprecedented pace of displacement has made the response difficult.

### Clinton pledges $110 million in U.S. aid

In Washington, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton announced a **$110 million humanitarian aid package** for displaced Pakistanis, saying the United States would provide food, water, shelter and other emergency assistance to those uprooted by the fighting.

Clinton said the aid was intended to support civilians caught in the conflict, emphasizing that Pakistanis fleeing militant violence needed immediate international help. The pledge included emergency relief supplies as well as support for the United Nations and nongovernmental organizations working on the ground.

The U.S. announcement came as the Obama administration sought to strengthen Pakistan’s civilian government while encouraging Islamabad to sustain pressure on Taliban-linked militants. American officials have described Pakistan’s northwest as a critical front in the fight against extremism, but they have also warned that mishandling the displacement crisis could undermine public support for the military campaign.

For many displaced families, however, geopolitical concerns are distant compared with immediate needs: food for children, medical care for the sick, and assurances that they will one day be able to return home safely.

### Fighting continues in Buner district

Meanwhile, the latest fighting has continued in **Buner district**, a strategically significant area roughly 60 miles from Islamabad that alarmed Pakistani and Western officials when Taliban fighters moved into the district earlier in 2009. Their advance raised fears that militants were expanding beyond Swat and challenging the authority of the state across a broader region.

Pakistani security forces have been engaged in operations to clear militants from Buner’s towns, villages and mountain hideouts. The terrain has made the fighting difficult, with militants using ridgelines, tunnels and fortified positions to resist government forces. Military officials have reported clashes in parts of the district as troops moved to regain control of roads and population centers.

The fighting in Buner has added to the civilian flight from the region. Residents have described artillery fire, helicopter gunships and house-to-house searches, as well as Taliban intimidation and restrictions before the military operation began. Many families said they delayed leaving because they feared traveling through combat zones, only to flee once the fighting moved closer.

Pakistan’s military has said its operations are aimed at restoring government control and eliminating militants who had exploited a failed peace deal in Swat to expand their influence. Under that agreement, authorities had accepted the implementation of Islamic law in parts of the Malakand region, but Taliban fighters continued pushing into neighboring areas, prompting the army to launch a broader offensive.

### Anger in camps, uncertainty at home

The humanitarian emergency has exposed deep anxiety among civilians who say they feel trapped between militants and the military. Some displaced residents blame the Taliban for bringing war to their communities; others criticize the government for not evacuating civilians sooner or preparing enough shelter before launching major operations.

Camp protests have reflected that frustration. Displaced families have demanded better facilities, faster delivery of relief and clearer information about missing relatives and return plans. In some areas, authorities have tried to calm tensions by increasing police presence and promising expanded aid distribution.

But relief workers say the crisis is likely to worsen unless more resources arrive quickly. With summer heat rising and families packed into temporary shelters, the risks are growing. Children are especially vulnerable to dehydration, diarrhea and respiratory infections, and pregnant women face limited access to safe medical care.

The longer the fighting continues, the more difficult the displacement crisis becomes. Even if military operations succeed in pushing militants out of contested districts, many civilians may be unable to return quickly because of destroyed homes, unexploded ordnance, damaged roads and fears of renewed militant activity.

For Pakistan, the emergency is both a humanitarian disaster and a political challenge. The government’s ability to care for those displaced by the war could prove crucial to maintaining public support for the offensive — and to preventing militants from exploiting anger among uprooted communities.

For now, hundreds of thousands of Pakistanis remain in limbo, waiting in camps, schools and relatives’ homes, uncertain whether the next news from Buner or Swat will bring word of victory, more fighting, or another wave of families on the road.
